Field studies of the Pygmy short-horned lizard (Phrynosoma douglasii) conducted under controlled thermal conditions have provided detailed insights into its reproductive biology. When maintained at a constant temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], this species exhibits a well-defined pattern of egg production. Females typically produce between 3 and 15 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 15 eggs per clutch], constituting their entire annual reproductive output with a single clutch laid each year [F_R_i = single clutch laid each year]. This modest clutch size is characteristic of the genus and reflects a conservative life-history strategy suited to the unpredictable, arid environments these lizards inhabit. The incubation period under these same warm conditions lasts for several months, culminating in the emergence of miniature, fully-formed offspring. Newly emerged hatchlings are remarkably small, possessing a wet body mass at birth of just 0.8 grams [Wwb = 0.8 grams]. This minuscule initial size places them among the smallest neonates of any North American phrynosomatid, imposing a formidable challenge as they must rapidly locate food and shelter to evade predation during their vulnerable first weeks of life.

At the species' preferred body temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], juvenile Pygmy short-horned lizards undergo a period of rapid mass gain heavily dependent upon prey availability. The progression toward reproductive maturity is tightly linked to the accumulation of sufficient body reserves. Field records indicate that females reach the onset of puberty at a wet mass of approximately 10 grams [Wwp = approximately 10 grams], a threshold that represents a substantial increase from their birth size but is still only a fraction of the maximum adult mass. This milestone typically occurs within the first year of life for individuals that experience favorable thermal conditions and plentiful ant and beetle larvae supplies. The time since birth at which this pubertal transition occurs has been documented as 365 days since birth [tp = 365 days since birth] under these conditions, although variation is observed depending on local resource abundance and the duration of the active season in high-elevation habitats at a temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C].

The ultimate body size attained by adult Pygmy short-horned lizards reflects a slow, conservative growth trajectory that prioritizes survival over rapid mass accumulation. Data from mark-recapture studies across multiple populations in the Pacific Northwest indicate that the maximum recorded wet body mass in adults is 36 grams [Wwi = 36 grams]. This value is modest compared to other members of the Phrynosoma genus and is likely an adaptation to the cooler, high-elevation environments these lizards occupy, where metabolic costs are lower but prey is comparatively scarce. Sexual dimorphism in ultimate body size is minimal in this species, though gravid females may temporarily exceed this mass due to the retention of developing eggs. The attainment of such a mass is a protracted process, sometimes requiring several years of intermittent feeding during brief summer activity windows. This energetic constraint may also explain the relatively small clutch sizes observed, as females must partition limited resources between their own somatic needs and the production of heavily yolked, parchment-shelled eggs.

Longevity records for the Pygmy short-horned lizard underscore its position at the slow end of the phrynosomatid life-history spectrum. The maximum lifespan for individuals maintained under optimal conditions at 35 °C [T = 35 °C] has been recorded as 10 years [am = 10 years], a remarkable duration for a lizard of this body size. This extended lifespan is made possible by a suite of behavioral and physiological adaptations, including cryptic coloration that reduces predation risk and a low metabolic rate that conserves energy during the long winter brumation period. In the wild, achieving such an age is rare due to high predation pressure from snakes, birds of prey, and small carnivores, but individuals that survive to adulthood often enjoy several years of reproductive opportunity. The survival benefits of reaching a large body size are clear, as larger adults are less vulnerable to gape-limited predators and can store more fat reserves to survive periods of food scarcity in their harsh, high-desert and sagebrush-steppe habitats.

A contrasting pattern of pubertal development has been observed in some populations of Pygmy short-horned lizard, particularly those inhabiting lower-elevation sites with a longer active season. In these warmer locales, where basking opportunities are more abundant and invertebrate prey remains available for a greater portion of the year, juvenile growth rates are accelerated. Consequently, a secondary record for the time since birth at which sexual maturation occurs has been documented at 730 days since birth [tp = 730 days since birth] when animals are held at a constant 35 °C [T = 35 °C]. This alternative developmental schedule, which involves a full two-year delay before the onset of puberty, suggests that some individuals may forgo an early reproductive attempt to invest in continued somatic growth. By achieving a larger body size before their first breeding season, these delayed-maturing females can produce a clutch of 3 to 15 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of 3 to 15 eggs] that are larger and have a higher hatching success rate, potentially compensating for the lost reproductive opportunity of the previous year.
